newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch cautious as they move into EU hot-seat.
newsitem.headline: Dutch cautious as they move into EU hot-seat.

text.p: The Netherlands takes over the European Union presidency on Wednesday as well as responsibility for revising the 15-member bloc's Maastricht Treaty which it brokered five years ago.

With a heavy dual mandate to complete the inter-governmental conference (IGC) treaty review and keep Europe on track for a single currency, the Dutch are being cautious and pragmatic about their chances of success.
As it prepares for its 10th EU presidency in 40 years, The Hague is ditching idealism for realism.
"The European agenda has so much on it that there's really no room left for specific desiderata of our own," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said last week.
Agreement earlier this month on a stability pact to enforce budgetary discipline under Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has taken the heat out of one potential obstacle to Dutch success.

But they still have to hammer out the nuts-and-bolts of institutional reform to take the bloc's 370 million citizens into the 21st century and pave the way for a workable EU which plans to embrace several former-Communist states.

Key issues here include bringing in qualified majority voting to make the decision-making process easier; deciding how many Commissioners each member state should have in a larger bloc and giving greater powers to the European Parliament.

Prime Minister Wim Kok, who will champion the cause of the bloc's smaller nations, has vowed to push his 14 EU partners towards a safer, more decisive and democratic Europe, with clear foreign policy goals and a united front against organised crime.

The Dutch must also oversee further preparations for monetary union, due in 1999, hammering out the stability pact details, working on a revamped euro-linked exchange rate mechanism (ERM-II) and unveiling the new euro coins.
The Netherlands, one of the most pro-European of EU states, favours Germany's more flexible approach to EU integration, letting members forge ahead in some areas at different speeds.
"Countries which are unwilling or unable to take part...must not prevent others from going further. That's what I mean by a flexible Europe," Kok said recently.
But the biggest single headache will be the British general election, which could be held just five weeks ahead of the planned Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.
A poll triumph for the new-look Labour Party, out of office since 1979, would give the incoming British government precious little time to prepare for landmark treaty reforms in Europe.

"If the United Kingdom maintains all its current positions then there's not much chance of a substantive treaty," Van Mierlo said, adding: "We're pinning our hopes on some room for negotiation after the elections."
Britain's ruling Conservative Party is sharply divided over the EU with many so-called Euro-sceptics arguing that an anti-EU campaign is about the only way the party can hold on to power.

The Dutch are only cautiously optimistic about agreeing a Amsterdam treaty by mid-June. The Hague is still traumatised by the "Black Monday" diplomatic debacle when, in September 1991, all their partners bar one vetoed a draft Maastricht Treaty.
Already some expect the task to be handed on to Luxembourg to be wound up in the second half of the year.
"We learned our lesson (in Maastricht). We said in 1991 that we would take the initiative and make things happen. We won't make the mistake again..," said one diplomat.
While IGC and EMU will occupy diplomats' main efforts, one quintessentially Dutch issue, drugs, will grab media attention.

Improved Franco-Dutch ties, which led to a deal to harmonise Europe's fight against drugs and crime, have eased fears that a long-running rift over soft drug sales in Dutch "coffee-shops" could scupper progress on weightier issues.
But some here say the Dublin deal is not the last word on an issue that has driven a wedge between the Dutch and the rest.
In January, the Dutch will launch the European Year against Racism and in April will host a follow-up to the Barcelona Conference on closer EU ties with Mediterranean countries.
